title: Thomasin McKenzie, Finn Cole and Antony Starr to Lead Folklore Retelling ‘The Lie of Sherwood Forest,’ Logical and Protagonist Launching at AFM (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The legend of Robin Hood is set to be given a new retelling in “The Lie of Sherwood Forest,” launching at the upcoming AFM with Logical Pictures In
body:
The legend of Robin Hood is set to be given a new retelling in “The Lie of Sherwood Forest,” launching at the upcoming AFM with Logical Pictures International and Protagonist Pictures handling sales. 

	The film — coming from German production company augenschein and beginning production on Nov. 9 — is being directed by Patrick Vollrath (“7500,” “Subversion”) and will star Thomasin McKenzie (“Victorian Psycho,” “The Testament of Ann Lee”), Finn Cole (“Peaky Blinders,” “Last Breath”) and Antony Starr (“The Boys,” “The Covenant”).
	

	Smylie Bradwell (“Faith,” “Hamnet”), Brian Vernel (“The Odyssey,” “Slow Horses”) and Richard Durden (“Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker”) are also among the cast.

	Harris Kauffman wrote the screenplay, based on a story by Joachim Hedén and Patrick Vollrath.

	According to the description, “The Lie of Sherwood Forest” transforms the “familiar folklore into a “grounded, hard-hitting fight for survival, loyalty and justice, bringing a contemporary edge to one of storytelling’s most enduring figures.”

	The story sees Robin Hood and his companions deceived by a young woman into undertaking a daring mission to rescue her captured brother, an operation that spirals into a perilous heist. As loyalties fracture and hidden motives emerge, the outlaws must confront the true cost of their choices — and the price of challenging those in power. As per the synopsis: “But what begins as one desperate lie will inadvertently change the course of the legend forever.”

	“‘The Lie of Sherwood Forest’ is a radical new take of one of the world’s most enduring legends, reinvented as a bold, visceral and relentlessly propulsive film,” said Dave Bishop, CEO of Protagonist Pictures. “Patrick Vollrath will deliver an electrifying cinematic vision to a story that turns mythology on its head, combining gripping set pieces with genuine moral complexity.”
	

	Added Andrei Kamarowsky, head of international at Logical Pictures Group: “What immediately drew us to ‘The Lie of Sherwood Forest’ was the ingenuity and novelty of its premise: one young woman’s desperate deception sets Robin Hood and his outlaws on a dangerous journey that will ultimately reshape the myth. It remains true to the spirit of the original folklore while bringing a fresh perspective, real emotional stakes, and unrelenting tension.”

	The film is produced by augenschein’s Maximilian Leo, Jonas Katzenstein and Daniel Sonnabend, in co-production with ZDF and with funding support by Film- und Medienstiftung NRW, German Federal Film Fund (DFFF), German Federal Film Board (FFA), German Films, European Investment Fund and Creative Europe Media.

	“Our collaboration with Patrick on 7500 was a defining moment for augenschein, and we’ve been excited to find the right opportunity to work together again.” said Katzenstein. “Having developed the idea with Patrick, we’re thrilled to partner once more on this action thriller.”

	Added company partner Leo: “The film builds on the edge-of-your-seat tension and visceral, grounded action that defined 7500, taking those elements to an exciting new level within the world of Robin Hood.”

	Augenschein and Logical Pictures Group will finance, and the group’s sales subsidiary Logical Pictures International LPI will co-rep sales alongside Protagonist Pictures. Protagonist’s Bishop, George Hamilton and James Pugh serve as executive producers, while Frédéric Fiore, Ryan Wickers, and Kamarowsky will be executive producers for Logical Pictures Group.

	Thomasin McKenzie is represented by Untitled and CAA.Finn Cole is represented by UTA , Independent Talent Group, Sloane and Viewpoint PR. Antony Starr is represented by UTA, Auckland Actors, Impression Entertainment and Kovert Creative.

title: Stocks Rally Higher After Democrats Flip Congress
description: Wall Street cheered the Blue Wave that put Democrats in control of both the Senate and House, with major market indexes and media stocks posting ga
body:
Wall Street cheered the Blue Wave that put Democrats in control of both the Senate and House, with major market indexes and media stocks posting gains Wednesday morning after the midterm elections.

	The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared over 1,100 points in early trading, up 2.2%, to nearly 53,000, while the Nasdaq Composite index was up 2.4%. Analysts said the Democrats’ sweeping congressional win cleared away political uncertainty — and investors were bullish on the likely gridlock in D.C. keeping policies unchanged.
	

	“Still more uncertainty looms, but one thing is certain, there will be gridlock and historically this is good for the market,” Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, told CNBC. Woods said the market uptick also partly stemmed from President Donald Trump’s “initial tone and reaction to the results,” after Trump told the New York Times he would accept the midterm election results.

	As of Wednesday morning, Democrats held a 54-44 edge in the Senate over Republicans, with two races (in Mississippi and Alaska) yet to be called, according to the AP. In the House, Dems had secured 228 seats — giving the party a clear majority — and the GOP stood at 139, with outcomes in 68 races still undetermined.

	Media stocks that gained in early trading the morning after the midterms included Netflix (+4%), Comcast (+4%), Disney (+3.8%), Skydance (+2.8%) and Fox Corp. (+2.4%). Big tech stocks — despite analysts warning that Democratic majorities in Congress could create headwinds for AI data center buildouts — also rose: Apple (+6%) Amazon (7.6%), Alphabet (+4.9%) and Meta (+2.4%) all were trending higher.
	

	“The U.S. midterms are a political tornado,” Mike Bell, head of strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, told the Times. “But for all the political whirlwinds that the vote is likely to stir, the markets are less likely to be blown around by this result.”

	Not all stocks got a boost. Shares of Elon Musk’s SpaceX were down 1.3% in morning trading and Tesla’s stock was off -2.4%. Musk, the world’s wealthiest individual, spent at least $474 million backing Republican candidates, per CNBC, including $224 million toward the campaign of Texas attorney general Ken Paxton in the contest for the open Senate seat in Texas — which Democrat James Talarico won by a 12-point margin. Voters in Texas also elected Democratic contender Gina Hinojosa governor, who unseated incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott.

	“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk posted on X late Tuesday night, followed by a shrug emoji.

	Also falling post-election were shares of Trump Media & Technology Group, the operator of Truth Social (Trump’s primary social media platform). TMTG stock was trading down more than 10% in Wednesday morning trading, pushing its market cap under $1.5 billion. The Trump family trust owns 41% of Trump Media, Reuters reported last month.

schema.headline: Stocks Rally Higher After Democrats Flip Congress

title: ‘Merry Everything’ Variety Series Featuring Jennie Garth, John Legend and Lori Loughlin to Lead QVC+’s Holiday TV Lineup (EXCLUSIVE)
description: QVC has unveiled its 2026 holiday programming lineup for subcription-free streamers QVC+ and HSN+, anchored by new variety series featuring celebri
body:
QVC has unveiled its 2026 holiday programming lineup for subcription-free streamers QVC+ and HSN+, anchored by new variety series featuring celebrity guest stars like Jennie Garth, John Legend and Lori Loughlin.

	Hosted by QVC staple Chelsea Phillips Reid, “Merry Everything!” is described as a “joyful holiday variety series brings together QVC’s biggest personalities and special guests for a festive mix of décor, gifting, recipes, music, and seasonal entertaining.” 
	

	Per QVC+’s description for the show, “Merry Everything!” “delivers an upbeat, personality-driven experience designed to entertain viewers while inspiring holiday shopping. From Christmas cocktails and tree-trimming ideas to gift wrapping, recipes, and musical moments, each segment adds warmth, fun, and fresh inspiration. The result is a feel-good seasonal event that celebrates the holidays in a way only QVC+ & HSN+ can. Episodes will also allow guests to talk about their holiday traditions and how they have evolved over their lifetime as well discuss their favorite tablescapes, recipes and product must-haves.”

	Featuring guests including Garth, Legend, Loughlin, Laurie Felt, Kim Gravel, Mally, Shawn Killinger and Beekman Boys, “Merry Everything!” will debut Nov. 6 and air a total of four episodes on a bi-weekly schedule.

	See below for descriptions of more of QVC’s holiday 2026 programming lineup for QVC+ and HSN+, each provided by QVC.

	Cart Blanche Holiday12/1 – Special Guest Laura Gellar12/15 – Special Guest Dennis Basso

	Life’s a blank check, shouldn’t you spend it on what you love? That’s exactly what program host John Battagliese is asking in Cart Blanche. That’s Cart, without the “e.” Because this is QVC, after all. In each episode John is giving his popular guests free rein (and vocal support) to be who they want to be, talk about what they want to talk about whether it’s the latest in pop culture or personal tidbits, and maybe even buy a little something along the way. Special holiday episodes will air this December with guests Laura Gellar & Dennis Basso.
	

	Additionally, November will feature fashion model Coco Rocha (11/3) and The Real Housewives Of Rhode Island’s Rosie DiMare (11/17).

	Present Pop-UpOngoing across holiday seasonRotating Hosts Tori Mistic, Steve Doss and Lisa Tancredi

	The holiday season is upon us, as is the annual question: what does everyone hope to see under the tree? We’ve got the hits that are sure to be at the top of their lists in Present Pop-Up, a QVC+ and HSN+ original series. Unwrap a list of our own, full of curated finds for those friends and family that are impossible to shop for, including some of today’s most buzzworthy gifts from the 2026 QVC Gift Guide—and shop them straight from your screen, no sleigh or reindeer required.

	David’s Recipe CornerHosted by David VenableSundays at Noon EST

	QVC’s Resident Foodie and Best-Selling Cookbook Author David Venable shares his enthusiasm for food, fun, and everything a home cook needs to create great meals and memories throughout this holiday season.

	Each edition finds David whipping up his favorite recipes, cooks with culinary greats, and helps you build a better kitchen with innovative appliances, kitchenware, and cookbooks. Whether you’re a beginner cook or a seasoned chef, it’s time to get comfortable in the kitchen. It’s one big celebration of great cooking and delicious food.

	LifeStyledNew episodes every Wednesday

	Are you suffering from inspiration frustration this holiday season? Is your dream aesthetic just…well, a dream? No more! It’s time to make your vision a reality during LifeStyled. Whether you’re picturing something mild, wild, or anywhere in between, we’re got the simple steps and on-trend finds to take your look from drab to fab. Level up everything from your wardrobe to your home as you shop leading brands in fashion, decor, and more that effortlessly elevate your space and give you the look you’ve been searching for.

title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Audience Award at London Film Festival
description: “La Bola Negra,” the queer historical drama from Spanish filmmaking duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, collectively known as Los Javis, has won
body:
“La Bola Negra,” the queer historical drama from Spanish filmmaking duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, collectively known as Los Javis, has won the audience award at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival.

	The film, which stars Penélope Cruz, Glenn Close and Miguel Bernardeau, has also earned a nomination for best international independent film at the British Independent Film Awards (BIFAs) ahead of its U.K theatrical release. 


	The latest recognition follows the film’s U.K. premiere at the London Film Festival on Oct. 8, where it played to sold-out audiences. Previous recipients of the festival’s audience award include Chloé Zhao’s “Hamnet” in 2025, “Four Mothers” in 2024 and “Gassed Up” in 2023.
	

	“We are absolutely delighted that ‘La Bola Negra’ has won the BFI London Film Festival Audience Award,” Calvo and Ambrossi said in a joint statement. “It was a real pleasure to bring the film to London in October, and we are incredibly grateful to everyone who came to see it and voted for us. To receive this recognition from audiences is particularly meaningful.”

	Inspired by the unfinished final work of Spanish poet and playwright Federico García Lorca and a play by Alberto Conejero, “La Bola Negra” follows three men whose lives are connected across three different periods: 1932, 1937 and 2017. Spanning three generations, the film explores queer identity, forbidden love and the ways personal histories are preserved or erased over time.

	The ensemble cast also includes Lola Dueñas, Carlos González and Spanish musician Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his feature film acting debut.

	The ensemble cast also includes Lola Dueñas, Carlos González and Spanish musician Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his feature film acting debut.

	Spain has additionally selected the film as its official submission for best international feature at the 2027 Academy Awards.

	Calvo and Ambrossi previously created the acclaimed Spanish television series “Veneno,” which chronicled the life of transgender icon Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez, as well as the musical comedy series “Paquita Salas.” Their latest feature continues the filmmakers’ exploration of queer identity and overlooked histories on a larger, decades-spanning scale.

	Altitude will release “La Bola Negra” in U.K. and Irish cinemas on Nov. 6.

title: Tinto Brass, Director of Erotic Epics ‘Caligula’ and ‘Salon Kitty,’ Dies at 93
description:
Italian director Tinto Brass, known for the historic erotic epics “Salon Kitty” and “Caligula,” has died. He was 93.

	Brass’ family announced the
body:
Italian director Tinto Brass, known for the historic erotic epics “Salon Kitty” and “Caligula,” has died. He was 93.

	Brass’ family announced the news of his death on Wednesday to Italian press agency Ansa.

	Born in Milan in 1933 to a Venetian family of artists, Brass first studied law before veering towards film during the late 1950s. He wound up as an archivist at the Cinémathèque Francais in Paris, where he met Roberto Rossellini and worked as an assistant on Rossellini’s war drama “General della Rovere.”
	

	Brass made his directorial debut in 1963 with the Venice-set tale “In Capo Al Mondo,” later retitled “Chi Lavora è Perduto,” about a young unemployed man with antisocial tendencies that received enthusiastic acclaim at the Venice Film Festival. The film, however, ran into big problems with Italian censors in what became the first of many battles Brass faced with censorship for various reasons.

	Brass spent the large part of the late 1960s and early 1970s in London shooting several English-language films, including 1967 erotic pop thriller “Deadly Sweet,” starring Jean-Louis Trintignant and Sweden’s Ewa Aulin. Trintignant stars as a young man who discovers that his business contact has been murdered. Instead of calling the police, he decides to protect a young woman, played by Aulin, at the crime scene and pursue the real killers‚ which puts him on a collision course with the London underworld.

	“Deadly Sweet” was presented out-of-competition at the 1967 Venice International Film Festival. The restored version played at Venice earlier this year as a tribute to Brass. It was followed by “Attraction” (1969) and “Dropout” (1970).
	

	Brass broke out internationally with erotic war drama “Salon Kitty” (1976), set in a high-class Berlin brothel used by the Nazi intelligence service and starring Helmut Berger. But his best known film outside Italy is “Caligula,” which was made in 1979 and released in 1984 in a different cut from that intended by Brass. The contentious film was self-financed in 1980 by Penthouse founder Bob Guccione, who after fighting with Brass and screenwriter Gore Vidal, wrested control of the project and tossed out the script. He added adult content that he shot after the actors — which included Helen Mirren, Malcolm McDowell, John Gielgud and Peter O’Toole — had finished their shoots, prompting Brass and Vidal to sue to have their names removed from the picture.

	In 1983, Brass helmed “The Key,” an adaptation of a novel by Japanese author Tanizaki Junichiro starring Stefania Sandrelli, in a move towards more highbrow eroticism that played well globally. It was followed by other works focused on the journey of sexual liberation of their female characters, including “Black Angel” (2002) and “Fallo” (2003).

	Brass is survived by his wife, Caterina Varzi, and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass.

title: Thessaloniki Film Festival Chief Hopes Event Can Help ‘Ease Pain’ in ‘Difficult’ Times: ‘Cinema Matters’
description: The Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival kicks off its 67th edition this week with an eclectic lineup of festival favorites, Oscar hopefuls and homegro
body:
The Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival kicks off its 67th edition this week with an eclectic lineup of festival favorites, Oscar hopefuls and homegrown films that showcase the range and dynamism of the Greek industry.

	But on the eve of this year’s event, artistic director Orestis Andreadakis admits that it’s far from business as usual at the long-running fest.

	“This year’s festival takes place during one of the most difficult and volatile periods for humanity: wars, massacres, the rise of the far right and neo-fascism, social unrest, uncertainty about the development of artificial intelligence and the climate crisis,” Andreadakis tells Variety. “All of this is part of our shared reality, and of course it is reflected in this year’s selection.
	

	“We hope that through the films of the 67th TIFF we can offer a little hope, ease pain and resist horror, polarization, hostility and dehumanization,” he continues. “Films can broaden our horizons, sharpen our awareness and critical thinking, and shape us in unexpected ways.”

	The festival opens with “Minotaur,” by two-time Academy Award nominee Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan,” “Loveless”), a trenchant portrayal of despair and corruption in Vladimir Putin’s Russia that won the Grand Prix in Cannes and will represent France in the international feature film Oscar race. Describing it as a “a powerful and unsparing portrait of a society trapped in its own labyrinth of fear and moral compromise,” Andreadakis says the film was a “natural choice” for the programming team. 
	

	“It is exactly the kind of cinema we believe in: brave, demanding and able to sharpen our awareness of the world we live in,” he says. The festival closes Nov. 15 with “Woman Unknown,” the Venice Golden Lion winner from May el-Toukhy, with Venice best actress winner Mathilde Arcel in attendance.

	Among the other guests on hand in Thessaloniki will be Spanish filmmaker Oliver Laxe (“Sirat”), who won the festival’s Golden Alexander in 2019 with his Un Certain Regard prizewinner “Fire Will Come.” Laxe has been tapped to curate a special programming sidebar, “Welcome to the Desert,” and will also deliver a talk for festival audiences.

	Meanwhile, Turkish filmmaker Emin Alper will be feted with a tribute to his acclaimed body of work — including this year’s Berlinale Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize-winning, “Salvation” — while German director Fatih Akin will be on hand to present his latest film, “Ghost Song,” which opened the San Sebastian Film Festival. Greek composer and conductor Stavros Xarchakos and filmmaker Nikos Grammatikos will also receive honorary Golden Alexander Awards at this year’s event.



	

					Thessaloniki Film Festival artistic director Orestis Andreadakis
									Courtesy Olympia Krasagaki
	



	A total of 258 films will screen across the festival’s various sections, with 10 films vying for the Golden Alexander in the main international competition. Among them are Walter Thompson-Hernández’s Sundance-premiering “If I Go Will They Miss Me” and Sarah Arnold’s French caper comedy “Too Many Beasts,” which bowed at Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. Also competing is Brazilian directors Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho’s gay erotic thriller “The Riverbank,” which won prizes at Locarno and Rio.

	A trio of Greek films are also in the running for top honors, including Konstantina Kotzamani’s Un Certain Regard premiere “Titanic Ocean,” Efthimis Kosemund Sanidis’ Karlovy Vary competitor “A Whole Person Almost” and Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” which won the prize for best director in the Venice Film Festival’s Horizons strand. They’re among the 26 feature-length and 28 short films that will represent the host nation at its premier film event, showcasing the fact that, as Andreadakis puts it, “Greek cinema is in a great place right now.”
	

	“We are extremely happy, because this year a total of 26 Greek feature films will be screened at the festival, seven of them in our three international competition sections,” Andreadakis says. “The program includes the most exciting new voices in Greek cinema, as well as major, well-established filmmakers.”

	Supporting the Greek film business has always been a core part of the mission of the Thessaloniki Film Festival and its industry arm, Agora, with Andreadakis noting that “the festival does more than give a film a slot in its program.”

	“In Thessaloniki, members of the Greek film community (directors, producers, distributors, screenwriters, technicians and actors) can network, form international partnerships and find their way into international markets and festivals,” he says.

	They’re not alone, as the festival — coming at the tail end of the fall circuit — has become an increasingly popular gathering place for the international industry, particularly for filmmakers in the Eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea regions, while the Agora continues to expand its geographical footprint and foster collaborations with a range of partners from across Europe and beyond.

	It’s been 10 years since the respected writer and film critic was handed the reins of Greece’s oldest and most prestigious film festival, and as he looks back now, Andreadakis acknowledges that in the past decade the festival has “had to overcome a lot of challenges, the biggest being the COVID period, where we had to rethink the very idea of a film festival.”

	“We had to make difficult decisions, but it also showed us how much a festival is needed as a meeting point,” he says. “As not only the world, but also the way we experience film is changing rapidly, we hope that we can still continue to grow and change, without losing our focus. 

	“As audiences are watching films in new ways, we want to keep finding ways to bring people, especially younger audiences, back to the shared experience of the cinema,” he continues. “At the same time, we want to strengthen Agora even further and make Thessaloniki a key hub for European cinema, a place where projects are born, where new ideas surface, where collaborations take place. Our goal remains simple: to keep the festival a place where cinema is discovered and shared.”
	

	The Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

schema.headline: Thessaloniki Film Festival Chief Hopes Event Can Help ‘Ease Pain’ in ‘Difficult’ Times: ‘Cinema Matters’

title: Prime Video’s Superb Muhammad Ali Series ‘The Greatest’ Makes a Star Out of Newcomer Jaalen Best: TV Review
description: Some historical figures are so towering that they become mythical. Muhammad Ali, the athlete, the man, the activist, is one of them. Ali’s life was
body:
Some historical figures are so towering that they become mythical. Muhammad Ali, the athlete, the man, the activist, is one of them. Ali’s life was under the microscope while he was alive, and it has been chronicled during this century in films like 2001’s “Ali,” starring Will Smith, and Regina King’s 2020 film “One Night in Miami.” However, Prime Video’s “The Greatest,” offers a more grounded, nuanced portrait of a man whose family, talent and self-determination let him transcend boxing to become a global icon. From “Cross” creator Ben Watkins — and in collaboration with Ali’s estate and executive producers Michael B. Jordan and Shawn “Jay-Z” Carter — “The Greatest” is outstanding.The eight-episode series opens in 1960 in Rome. Miles away from his hometown of Louisville, Kentucky, 18-year-old Cassius Clay (an exemplary Jaalen Best) and his Olympic teammates explore the coliseum. Later, as his family tunes in via radio, Cassius wallops Poland’s Zbigniew Pietrzykowski in the ring and wins gold for the United States. Hours after the match, Cassius finds himself alone in a phone booth, calling home. When his mother, Odessa Clay (Dana Gourrier), whom he affectionately calls Bird, answers, the amateur boxer weeps in relief.These moments with Cassius’ family, who call him “G,” distinguish “The Greatest” from countless other biopics and series that have crossed our screens. Returning home with the glittering medal draped on his neck, Cassius is lauded but also thrust right back into the oppressive, segregated and deeply racist Louisville. Though his younger brother Rudy (Kai Parham) is eager to welcome his roommate and best friend back into the fold, and Odessa’s dinner spread rivals any Thanksgiving feast, the Clay household is not without its cracks and dark shadows. Stern and stoic with a simmering rage due to a lifetime of racial abuses and dreams unfulfilled, Cassius Clay Sr. (Omari Hardwick) has volatile mood changes. His love of his family is palpable, but his alcoholism, violent temper, philandering and anger are just as potent. By depicting the Clays in their full truth, “The Greatest” allows Cassius, later known as Muhammad Ali, to appear as a three-dimensional person on screen.The show chronicles the next four years of Cassius’ life, from his going pro to teaming up with his trainer, Angelo Dundee (Giovanni Ribisi); converting to Islam, and his friendship with Malcolm X (Michael Ealy) and his eventual victory over Sonny Liston (Amin Joseph) to become the Heavyweight Champion of the World in 1964. Yet, “The Greatest” is at its most profound when it lets viewers sit with Ali outside the boxing ring. In this series, he is, above all, a young Black man coming of age in Jim Crow America and defying every rule society set before him.While the entire cast is stellar, particularly Gourrier and Hardwick as loving parents who have done everything in their power to raise upstanding (and Christian) young men, Best’s turn as Ali, one of the most enigmatic figures in our history, is magnetic. He not only resembles the dynamic boxer in his face and stature, but his voice cadence, especially when he delivers quick-witted rhymes and riddles to taunt his opponents and hype himself up, is spot on. This a credit to Watkins, who was willing to find a relatively unknown actor and give him a platform to shine, which feels increasingly rare these days.The series also depicts several stunning boxing matches. From Floyd Patterson vs. Sonny Liston’s 1962 fight, where Liston earned the heavyweight title, to Ali’s 1963 fight against Henry Cooper in London, the outstanding camera work from cinematographers Stuart Campbell and Jeremy Benning captures enough blood and guts to make audiences feel like they’re right there in the ring with the fighters. Though “The Greatest” sprinkles in some hokier black-and-white vignettes to show the matches, passages of time or Cassius’ inner monologue, it always quickly returns to itself. The soundtrack even features contemporary artists like J. Cole and Kendrick Lamar, along with era-defining songs such as Nina Simone’s “To Be Young, Gifted and Black.”More than a show about men’s brawn, Watkins opens up the story, and lets viewers walk alongside Cassius, Malcolm X, Sonny Liston and Cassius Sr. These were Black men trying to stand tall in a society that didn’t see them as human. Weaving the narratives together creates a fuller picture of generations of men and women who, however imperfectly, did their best to carve out lives for themselves in a world determined to humiliate them. It’s especially interesting to see how Cassius and Rudy were drawn to Malcolm X and the Nation of Islam, then led by Elijah Muhammad (Hill Harper), which offered Black Americans a different view of themselves and America, though many had long been loyal to the Christian faith.“The Greatest” reminds us that history is ever-present. The show profiles a young man who defined himself with youthful arrogance and bold determination, and who would keep standing up for his convictions, even when it cost him everything. By laying the foundation for who Cassius Clay was, the series gives audiences a clearer sense of who Muhammad Ali became and why his presence is so enduring.
	
	All eight episodes of “The Greatest” premiere on Nov. 4 on Prime Video.

schema.headline: Prime Video’s Superb Muhammad Ali Series ‘The Greatest’ Makes a Star Out of Newcomer Jaalen Best: TV Review

title: How Thessaloniki’s Industry Arm Continues to Launch Regional Talent, Widen Its Focus With Partnerships ‘Across Europe and Beyond’
description: It’s been almost two decades since Thanos Stavropoulos, the Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival’s incoming industry head, was hired by the long-runnin
body:
It’s been almost two decades since Thanos Stavropoulos, the Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival’s incoming industry head, was hired by the long-running Greek fest as a programming assistant, assuming a variety of roles before taking the reins of its widely respected industry program this spring.

	That continuity is a hallmark of both the festival and its industry arm, Agora, and on the eve of this year’s event, Stavropoulos says he’s “committed to the same objective my predecessors served so very successfully” since the Agora launched in 2005. Namely, “to facilitate the growth of the local and regional industry through the establishment and continuous development of programs which will help bring the filmmakers and their projects out into the world,” he says.
	

	It’s a simple enough mission on its surface, but one that is facing unprecedented headwinds from a range of political, social and economic factors. This year’s event unfolds against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Palestine, fears of a widening war in Iran and the Middle East, social and economic unrest across Europe and much of the world — not to mention the industry-specific factors, such as the continued shake-ups and consolidations at studios in the U.S. and Europe, that only add to the lingering sense of uncertainty.

	“The world is a bit of a mess, isn’t it?” Stavropoulos deadpans. “We can do only so much from where we stand, as professionals in this particular industry.”

	What the Agora team can do more than anything is build bridges and create an environment for collaborations — the lifeblood of the European industry — to take root. “Our mission is to continue to aid, foster and support in any way we can the filmmakers — whether emerging or well-established — from the countries represented in the Agora and provide the platform for them to connect with partners from Europe and beyond,” says Stavropoulos.
	

	In ways big and small, the Agora continues to evolve with the times, allowing it to better meet the needs of both the industry and the festival audience. Its conversation series, which previously included closed sessions for industry guests, will now be open to all festivalgoers “with a curious mind and interests that go further than what’s on the cinema screen,” he says. 

	Meanwhile, a dedicated decompression room — inaugurated last year as part of a broader festival focus on mental health — will be bolstered by an Agora discussion on the importance of resolving conflict in creative collaborations. “The Agora is an ever-developing system, and like in nature, when the components of a habitat work together in harmony, it thrives,” Stavropoulos explains.

	One of the industry section’s most significant moves in recent years was the launch of a dedicated series strand in 2022, introducing a loaded program of talks and TV-focused sessions which Stavropoulos says has “grown and become more dynamic” and now takes place across the opening weekend of the festival.



	

					Thessaloniki industry head Thanos Stavropoulos
									Courtesy Thessaloniki Film Festival
	



	This year’s edition includes masterclasses from “American Crime Story: The Assassination of Gianni Versace” screenwriter Tom Rob Smith and Christopher Papakaliatis, creator of the hit Netflix series “Maestro in Blue.” Other sessions will assemble key players in the Greek TV ecosystem to unpack the future of Greek scripted television in the global landscape, and a focus on how to package and co-produce local series for the international market.

	Such talks come at a pivotal moment for TV creators in Greece, which was among the signees earlier this year of the historic European Convention that marks the first international treaty supporting the independent co-production of series for television and streaming platforms. “We want to catch that momentum and focus more on how we can help the local series industry and talents from Greece and the region benefit from this treaty,” Stavropoulos says.

	That includes plans for the Agora to launch a regional pitching platform for emerging and established screenwriters and their projects. “The region is so rich in original stories and absolutely wonderful talents which deserve more opportunities, more visibility and outlets for their creative energy to be channeled through,” Stavropoulos says.
	

	Nowhere are those stories and talents more evident than in the Crossroads Co-Production Forum and Agora Works in Progress, the Agora’s long-running strands for films from Southeast Europe, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea region. Stavropoulos cites a trio of Agora alumni playing at this year’s festival — “Black Money for White Nights,” by Kristina Grozeva and Petar Valchanov; “Hold Onto Me,” by Myrsini Aristidou; and “I Matter,” by Alina Șerban — as evidence of the event’s track record: All three have been short-listed for the next European Film Awards, to be held in Athens, while Aristidou’s Sundance-awarded debut (pictured, top) marks the first ever Cypriot submission for the Oscars.

	Looking over this year’s lineup, Stavropoulos highlights “a wide variety of themes, different filmmaking styles and intriguing visual approaches,” with new projects from Tribeca prizewinner Darko Lungulov (“Here and There”), Serbian director Nikola Ležaić (“Tilva Roš”) and Egyptian filmmakers and 2024 Variety MENA Talents of the Year Ayman El Amir and Nada Riyadh (“The Brink of Dreams”) being presented to an audience of industry professionals.

	“We’ll venture in every direction and move towards every horizon: from Beirut to the moon and then time travel to the ’80s. Then we sling back to today to hear a dark story from the early years of the 20th century,” he says. “There’s no particular geography; our projects’ creative teams’ visions and dreams go above and beyond space and time.”

	As he settles into his new role, Stavropoulos is already looking ahead to how he can leave his mark on the Agora, insisting that the process will likely involve fine-tuning the event’s already proven formula.

	“What we will certainly continue to do is sustainably grow. Our size will not change. But we will reach out further into the world and our circle of friends will widen,” he says. “The target remains the same: to connect, network and create opportunities for the local and regional film professionals. Our modus operandi remains the same: we will continue providing a space that is safe and offers for meaningful, trusting and productive partnerships.

	“Thessaloniki sits at the very crossroads of the wider region of Southeast Europe and the Mediterranean,” he adds, “and the Agora is the natural place for these connections to begin and to grow.”
	

	The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

schema.headline: How Thessaloniki’s Industry Arm Continues to Launch Regional Talent, Widen Its Focus With Partnerships ‘Across Europe and Beyond’

title: Bill Nighy, Hayley Atwell and Maisie Williams Lead Voice Cast of Animated Feature ‘The Last Dino’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Bill Nighy (“Living,” “Love Actually”), Hayley Atwell (“Mission: Impossible,” “Captain America”) and Maisie Williams (“Game of Thrones”) have joine
body:
Bill Nighy (“Living,” “Love Actually”), Hayley Atwell (“Mission: Impossible,” “Captain America”) and Maisie Williams (“Game of Thrones”) have joined the English-language voice cast of “The Last Dino,” the upcoming CG-animated family feature directed by Federico Milella.

	The film will make its market premiere at the American Film Market next week, ahead of its planned international theatrical releases in 2027.
	



	

					“The Last Dino”
									Courtesy of Fabrique d’Images
	



	International sales are handled by Global Constellation, a Vuelta company, which has already secured distribution deals across multiple territories.

	“The Last Dino” follows Rex, the son of the King of Dinosaurs, who is unexpectedly catapulted 65 million years into the future, landing in a world where dinosaurs are extinct, being smart matters more than being strong, and being king of the jungle means absolutely nothing. 

	Determined to find his way home, Rex teams up with an unlikely crew of friends for a wild adventure that challenges everything he thought he knew about strength, friendship and family. Along the way, he discovers that family isn’t necessarily about where you come from, but about who stands by your side, and that sometimes the greatest adventure isn’t finding your way home, but finding where you truly belong.

	The film will be released in France (KMBO), the U.K. and Ireland (Sky Original), Australia and New Zealand (Umbrella), Benelux (WWE), Portugal (Nos Audiovisuais), Poland (Forum Film), Hungary (Vertigo), the Czech and Slovak Republics (FoxxMedia), Bulgaria (ProFilm), the former Yugoslavia (MCF Megacom), Baltics & Ukraine (Ad Astra), Greece and Cyprus (Filmtrade), Israel (Red Cape), Turkey and the Middle East and North Africa (Italia Film), Vietnam (Mockingbird), and Latin America (BF Distribution).
	

	Written by Ben Smith (“StarDog and TurboCat”), “The Last Dino” is produced by Luxembourg-based animation studio Fabrique d’Images, in co-production with Belgium-based Freaks Factory (“Spiked”), U.K.-based Terrible Lizard Productions and Broadvision Perspectives India. The production is supported by Film Fund Luxembourg and Wallimage (Wallonia).

	Global Constellation’s Fabien Westerhoff said: “’The Last Dino’ combines irresistible slapstick comedy with heartfelt storytelling in a hugely entertaining time-travelling adventure for the family. At its core is a universal message about embracing our differences, finding our tribe and discovering where we truly belong. We’re delighted to present the film to buyers at AFM ahead of its international theatrical rollout in 2027.”

schema.headline: Bill Nighy, Hayley Atwell and Maisie Williams Lead Voice Cast of Animated Feature ‘The Last Dino’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market
description: Paris Creator Week is doubling in size this year, drawing 8,000 industry professionals and top executives from YouTube, Twitch, LinkedIn and tradit
body:
Paris Creator Week is doubling in size this year, drawing 8,000 industry professionals and top executives from YouTube, Twitch, LinkedIn and traditional media giants including Banijay and Mediawan. 

	The gathering kicks off today at the Halle de la Villette where a new study is being unveiled, revealing that the global creator economy is on track to reach $217.3 billion in 2026, marking a 26.2% year-on-year increase. The market, which has nearly tripled in size over the last five years, is projected to reach a staggering $1.22 trillion by 2033.
	

	France has emerged as a major international hub for the booming creator economy which will reach $10.1 billion locally this year, up 23.7% from 2025. It could more than double to $24.3 billion by 2030, per the study. That makes France the world’s seventh-largest creator economy and the third-largest in Europe, behind the U.K. and Germany. The sector already accounts for 227,000 full-time equivalent jobs in France. 

	Marc Lesage-Moretti, a former Goldman Sachs vice president turned content creator, known online as Jokariz, who co-founded Paris Creator Week in 2024, says the findings underscore a dramatic shift in an industry which took time to be taken seriously.

	“In the United States, everyone was talking about the creator economy, but when I started using that term in France three years ago, people looked at me as though I was speaking Chinese to them,” Lesage-Moretti tells Variety in a zoom interview a few days before the start of the event. “They would say, ‘Oh, the creator economy? You mean 14-year-old kids making entertainment videos in their bedrooms on YouTube?’”
	

	“People hadn’t yet understood how much this industry was becoming professionalized,” he says, citing HugoDécrypte, the popular French digital news outlet, which now employs around 40 people, including journalists and human resources staff.

	The huge expansion of the Paris Creator Week this year underscores how the general perception has evolved. It’s grown from 4,000 participants last year to an expected 8,000 this year, while its exhibition space has increased fivefold, from 200 to 1,000 square meters. YouTube alone is taking a 100-square-meter stand, Lesage-Moretti points out. 

	The event is also becoming increasingly international, with overseas attendees accounting for 30% of participants. Global platforms including YouTube, Twitch, LinkedIn, Spotify and SoundCloud are sending senior executives, while traditional entertainment groups are joining discussions about the future of content creation, distribution and monetization.

	“The idea is to create the VivaTech of the creator economy,” says Lesage-Moretti, referring to the major Paris technology conference.

	Unlike consumer-facing creator conventions, Paris Creator Week is positioning itself as a B2B gathering where creators, media execs, platforms, brands, agencies and investors can explore partnerships and new business models.

	The event’s growing appeal also reflects a major shift in advertising spending. According to the study, sponsorships and commercial partnerships now account for 49.8% of the global creator economy, followed by advertising on creator content at 22.7% and paid subscriptions at 13.8%.

	Advertisers are expected to contribute $172.8 billion to the sector in 2026, representing 79.5% of total spending, while creators themselves receive an estimated $92.6 billion, or 42.6% of the overall market.

	“Commercial partnerships are the main driver of growth,” Lesage says. “Brands that traditionally invested their money in other media or advertising channels are redirecting those budgets toward content creators.”

	“And we’re not just talking about luxury brands. We’re talking about every kind of brand: banks, major corporations, large businesses. We have major companies that now handle their financial communications through content creators,” Lesage says, adding that the money from these partnerships goes directly from a company to a content creator without the platform taking a single euro.”
	

	The industry’s rapid expansion is also fueling a wave of M&A’s. According to the Paris Creator Week study, 70 acquisitions took place globally in the first half of 2026, up 23% from the same period last year. North America accounted for 64.3% of acquisition targets, compared with 27.1% for Europe.

	Paris Creator Week is dedicating an entire conference track to M&A, looking at how investors value creator-led businesses and manage the “key man risk,” when companies are built around a single personality.

	Lesage says some businesses closely tied to their founders have managed to attract investment. For instance, the French podcast company Legend which lured a Belgian fund at a valuation of €72 million.

	“These are businesses that people thought couldn’t be sold because they were too dependent on a single personality, but we’re seeing that’s not necessarily the case,” he says. 

	For Drew Baldwin, head of Prentiss Media, founder of Tubefilter and creator of the Streamy Awards, the next stage of growth will depend on whether creators can evolve from individual personalities into scalable media businesses.

	“I still think creators on social platforms, including YouTube, are renting audiences. They don’t own the audience,” Baldwin tells Variety. “And the creators who can figure out how to take their audience and own that relationship are the ones who are going to be able to build new businesses around that community.”

	Baldwin, who is leading a session comparing the European and American creator economies at the Paris confab, argues France is well positioned to see its local creator economy thrive, even if it’s currently lagging behind the U.S.

	“France has always been, culturally, a champion of independent voices,” he says. “French cinema has an outsized footprint considering the size of the country. You have the Cannes Film Festival. You have an extraordinary amount of production coming out of France.”

	“Now, the question is: Will they champion the entrepreneurial spirit? And I think the answer, when I look at Paris Creator Week, is yes.”

	Baldwin says the U.S. has been ahead of the curve because it’s got a “common language and a more unified advertising market that make it easier to scale businesses.”
	

	As in the film and television business, Baldwin anticipates some consolidation in the digital space as creators compete for budgets traditionally reserved for media companies.

	“Like with any maturation in the economy, there will be consolidation. There will be winners, and there will be those that close shop,” he says.

	The major challenge is to overcome the key man risk, says Baldwin, who points to MrBeast, Dhar Mann and the British creator collective the Sidemen as examples of creators building businesses capable of expanding beyond their original social media audiences.

	“Those who can scale, like the Sidemen, WatchTime Studios and Dhar Mann, are the ones who are going to be able to do large-scale media deals,” he says. “Instead of just using creator marketing budgets, they can unlock true media budgets, which are really big.”

	That convergence is starting to happen even in heavily regulated markets like France, where major production groups including Banijay and Mediawan are exploring opportunities in the creator economy alongside streaming platforms and broadcasters such as TF1, Netflix and Canal+.

	“Creators are increasingly interested in working with distributors and platforms beyond the ones where they originally built their audiences,” says Lesage-Moretti. “If you’re a YouTuber, it makes sense to be present across social media platforms to diversify, but it also makes sense to explore cinema.”

	Lesage-Moretti cites the landmark experiment of French YouTuber Inoxtag, whose documentary “Kaizen” was released by MK2 French theaters and sold around 300,000 tickets in a single day. It launched on the same day on YouTube where it generated 40 million or 50 million views overall.

	Baldwin is also using Paris Creator Week to formally launch Creator Kitchen, an initiative aimed at bringing together executives from traditional and new media.

	The Paris edition will include an intimate dinner at L’Envol, Michelin-starred chef Thibaut Spiwack’s rooftop restaurant at the Philharmonie de Paris, near the event’s venue.

	Guests include Twitch CEO Dan Clancy; Justine Ryst, managing director of YouTube France and Southern Europe; Gregg Bywalski, managing director of Webedia Creators; Vincent Grynbaum, managing director of Mediawan Thematics; Nielsen CFO Jessica Holscott; and Mathieu Gallet, managing director of Bourdin Media and chairman of the supervisory board of Les Echos.
	

	For Baldwin, the growing appetite for an industry-focused gathering like Paris Creators Week illustrates that the industry is becoming a fully fledged part of the entertainment biz.

	“Why are thousands of people coming to this? It’s not a fan event. This is the business of the creator economy,” he says. 

	Lesage-Moretti, who is still financing the event with co-founder and managing director Pierre Alary, says they’ve received outside interest but want to keep control.

	“The real question is what advantage an outside investor would bring us? We have a very clear roadmap and strategy for how we’re going to accelerate our international expansion,” he says. “France has always been able to attract people from all over the world to Cannes for the film festival. We think the same thing should happen in the creator economy.”

schema.headline: Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market

title: Hailey Bieber Says She Struggled With Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder After Son's Birth
description:
Hailey Bieber
                          I Struggled With Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
body:
Hailey Bieber
                          I Struggled With Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
                          ... After Son's Birth
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 4, 2026
                            6:38 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 4, 2026
                                7:20 AM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hailey Bieber is opening up about a super difficult time in her life ... following the birth of her and Justin Bieber's first child, Jack Blues.
      
    
            In an interview with Women's Wear Daily, Hailey said she experienced premenstrual dysphoric disorder ... "After I had my son, I struggled with that a bit, and there's just not a lot of conversation or research around it."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If you don't already know ... PDD can cause extreme mood shifts -- ranging from hopelessness to anxiety to anger.
      
    
            Hailey says ... "Conversation, for me personally, makes me feel less alone. When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we're dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Hailey and Justin welcomed Jack in August 2024 ... and the beauty mogul revealed that their child was definitely an unexpected pregnancy given another diagnosis she received.
      
    
            Hailey told the "SHE M.D." podcast in March 2026 that she has a uterine septum -- a condition that comes with higher miscarriage and infertility risks.
      
    
            While Hailey was initially concerned about her pregnancy with Jack ... she gave birth to a healthy child ... but it sounds like her postpartum was difficult.

title: James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa Celebrate Shocking Election Wins at Whataburger
body:
James Talarico & Gina Hinojosa
                          Whata-Win!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 4, 2026
                            6:47 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa won't be flipping burgers at Whataburger come January ... because they just turned Texas blue -- and celebrated at their state's popular fast-food chain.
      
    
            The senator-elect and governor-elect from the Lone Star State raised their oversized soda cups to the end of a stressful election season at a local Whataburger late Tuesday night ... all smiles while surrounded by their adoring supporters after some shocking election results.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Talarico waxed Ken Paxton ... but that wasn't even the big surprise in Texas. 
      

            Even more surprisingly ... Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott -- reportedly winning by a reported 7 points. Abbott has served as the governor of Texas since 2015 and was seeking a fourth term. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Talarico and Hinojosa's wins are part of a much larger blue wave that swept the nation Tuesday night. Democrats won back the Senate and the House by wide margins.
      
    
            Victory tastes sweet ... as sweet as a pair of large Whataburger fountain drinks, apparently!

            Cher took home the trophy in 1988 for her performance in "Moonstruck" ... after being nominated for the second time.

title: Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed Clowns JD Vance, Mike Rogers in Victory Speech
description:
Abdul El-Sayed
                          Enjoy Retirement, Mike ...
                          Can
body:
Abdul El-Sayed
                          Enjoy Retirement, Mike ...
                          Can't Wait to See You in January, JD!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 4, 2026
                            7:18 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Abdul El-Sayed used his victory speech to shout out his opponent in the Senate race in Michigan and the sitting vice president ... though he wasn't in a bridge-building mood.
      
    
            The senator-elect took the stage at his rally in Michigan early Wednesday morning -- after the tight race was finally called in his favor ... and he addressed both Mike Rogers and VP JD Vance onstage.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            First, Rogers ... El-Sayed wished him well in his retirement down in Florida -- saying he knows MR has a big house in Florida and two yachts he can focus on down there.
      
    
            He added, "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you again."
      
    
            El-Sayed then reflected on the sweet irony of VP Vance -- one of his most vocal critics -- being constitutionally obligated to swear him into the Senate.
      
    
            "JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January" ... before playing into Michigan's well-known rivalry with Ohio.
      
    
            He kept score onstage ... saying it's Wolverines 1 -- Buckeyes 0. El-Sayed went to the University of Michigan while Vance attended The Ohio State University.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Media reports have already announced El-Sayed as the winner of the race -- which experts predicted would be quite close -- by about 7 points. At the time of publication, Rogers has not delivered a concession speech.
      
    
            El-Sayed's gonna have to work with Republicans to get bills passed over the next 6 years ... but we expect he'll keep on gloating for a few more days.
